```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# The example images are a PNG (read with magick) and TIFFs (read and written
# with tiff); without them the code is shown but not run.
has_deps <- requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("tiff", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4,
                      eval = has_deps)
library(hyperannotatR)
```

A *mask* is the artefact that turns hand-drawn regions into something a
segmentation or classification pipeline can consume: an integer raster on the
same pixel grid as the image, where each pixel carries the identity of the
region it belongs to. In hyperannotatR the mask is the core deliverable, and
`at_mask()` is the function that produces it from an `annot_roi`, an
`annot_layer`, or a whole `annot_project`.

## Three mask types

`at_mask()` writes one of three rasters, chosen with `type`:

- **`"binary"`** — a logical matrix: `TRUE` wherever *any* region covers a
  pixel, `FALSE` elsewhere. Use it for foreground/background problems ("is this
  pixel annotated at all?").
- **`"labelled"`** — one distinct positive integer per ROI, assigned in draw
  order. Use it when individual objects must stay separable, e.g. instance
  segmentation where two adjacent tumour nests are different things.
- **`"multiclass"`** — one integer per *label class*, so every ROI sharing a
  label collapses to the same value. Use it for semantic segmentation, where you
  care about the class ("tumour", "stroma") and not the particular ROI.

Every mask is an `annot_mask`: a matrix with an attached `legend` tibble
(`value`, `label`, `layer`, `roi_id`, `n_px`, `colour`) plus `level`, `dims`,
`mask_type` and `mask_metadata` attributes; the last records how to read the
values (below). Read the legend back with `at_mask_legend()`.

## Encoding metadata and alignment

`attr(mask, "mask_metadata")` is a versioned semantic description. Schema 1
records `encoding`, `background`, `overlap`, a `grid` (`dims` in width/height
order, `level`, `origin`, and sampling `stride`), the full `codebook`, and
`source` provenance. Rasterisation uses origin `(0,0)` and stride `(1,1)`.
A nearest-neighbour preview records its sampled dimensions and stride plus
`preview$parent_grid`; its counts describe only sampled pixels.

Public type names remain unchanged. Ordinary multiclass masks use categorical
encoding: category `3` belongs only to class `3`. With `overlap = "bitor"`, codes
must be distinct positive powers of two and background must be zero. A sample
`3` then belongs to both class `1` and class `2`. Legends, statistics, previews,
polygonisation, and display use this same membership rule. Composite display
labels join their class names with ` + ` and use the mean class colour.
A supplied global `values` map survives even if some classes have no pixels;
those classes retain zero counts. Empty legends recover with typed columns.

Foreground codes cannot equal background. Binary rasterisation rejects a
requested background of `1`, including for empty masks. Other accepted binary
backgrounds become effective `FALSE`/`0`, matching the logical stored samples.
NPY imports remain integer arrays, including arrays declared binary.

Derivation uses each input's own background and anatomy membership, preserving
the full state codebook. Declared grids and durable source descriptors must
agree. Queue entry IDs are retained as provenance but need not match for two
annotations of the same source; reopened-image cache generations never establish
source equality. Display names alone are insufficient. Reader options are compared
exactly, including atomic types, names, dimensions, nesting, attributes and
formal S4 identity. Sidecars store options with `options_encoding = "typed-json-v2"`:
a versioned, data-only representation that also records each value's formal-object
flag. Supported atomic/list S4 values recover without class constructors or an
installed class definition. Numeric options retain 17-digit precision. Malformed
or future option encodings fail. Older untyped JSON and typed schema 1 cannot
prove that all option structure survived (schema 1 omitted formal-object flags):
these sources are marked `options_status = "legacy-json"` and derivation requires
an explicit alignment assertion, including after re-export. Likewise,
`options_inferred = TRUE` records guessed legacy reader options and cannot
establish verified alignment. Any supplied inference flag must be a single,
non-missing logical value; omitting it leaves explicitly recorded options
unchanged. For standalone masks
whose registration you know, pass `alignment = "assert"` to `at_mask_derive()`.
This records an explicit registration assertion without resampling. Different
matrix dimensions always fail. The default `alignment = "legacy"` only permits
unknown-source fallback when both masks have legacy metadata and records
`legacy-assumed`. Self-combination records `self-grid`, without claiming an
external source registration.

## The pixel-coverage contract

Rasterisation is only reproducible if the pixel/geometry relationship is exact,
so hyperannotatR pins it down. Pixel `(i, j)` covers the half-open square
`[j-1, j) x [i-1, i)`, with `(0, 0)` at the top-left corner of the top-left
pixel; its centre is therefore `(j - 0.5, i - 0.5)`. With the default
`touches = FALSE`, a pixel is in the mask when *its centre* lies inside the
polygon. Boundary ties use the symbolic sample `(x + epsilon, y + epsilon^2)`
as `epsilon` tends to zero from above; there is no finite coordinate shift.
At each centre y, edges are active on `[minY, maxY)` and sorted crossing pairs
fill `[left, right)`. For rectangles, lower edges count as inside and upper
edges as outside. For the triangle `(0,0), (5,0), (5,5)`, the diagonal `y = x`
counts as inside: its five rows contain 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1 pixels, respectively.
Hole rings remove pixels by parity regardless of ring orientation, and
MultiPolygon components combine by union. Thin polygons without selected
centres produce an empty mask. Single and batched masks and both engine choices
share this centre-membership rule.

Points use their half-open containing cell: point `(5,5)` selects matrix row 6,
column 6, because its cell is `[5,6) x [5,6)`. Multipoints select the union of
these cells. Extraction uses the same support and reads the corresponding
bounded image tile. These boundary rules correct the earlier finite-shift
behavior, which selected row 5, column 5 for an integer-coordinate point and
could produce inconsistent diagonal polygon coverage.

All-touched masks and line rasterisation retain the selected engine's behavior;
engine equality is guaranteed for centre-based polygons and points.

The cleanest way to trust this is to compute a small case by eye. Take a
rectangle from `(2, 2)` to `(5, 5)` on a 10x10 grid:

```{r worked}
r <- at_roi_rect(2, 2, 5, 5, label = "a")
m <- at_mask(r, "binary", dims = c(10, 10))
print(matrix(as.integer(m), 10, 10))
```

Rows and columns 3, 4 and 5 are set, and nothing else. The rectangle spans
`x` in `[2, 5)`; the pixel-centre x-coordinates that fall in that interval are
`2.5, 3.5, 4.5`, i.e. columns 3, 4, 5. The centre at `x = 5.5` (column 6) is
outside, and the lower edge at `x = 2` is inside because centre `2.5 > 2`. The
same reasoning on `y` gives rows 3:5. A rectangle three pixels wide and three
pixels high covers exactly nine pixels, with no fencepost surprises.

## `touches`: centres versus contact

`touches = TRUE` switches to a "does the polygon touch the pixel at all" rule
(GDAL `ALL_TOUCHED=TRUE`), which grows the region by the fringe pixels a polygon
merely clips. It matters when edges cut through pixel interiors rather than
running along the grid. A rectangle with fractional bounds shows the contrast:

```{r touches}
r2  <- at_roi_rect(2.5, 2.5, 4.5, 4.5, label = "a")
off <- matrix(as.integer(at_mask(r2, "binary", dims = c(8, 8), touches = FALSE)), 8, 8)
on  <- matrix(as.integer(at_mask(r2, "binary", dims = c(8, 8), touches = TRUE)),  8, 8)
off
on
```

With `touches = FALSE` only the pixels whose centres sit inside the rectangle
are kept; with `touches = TRUE` the partially clipped border pixels join too.
Prefer the default for area-faithful masks, and `touches = TRUE` only when you
must not drop thin structures.

## Overlap resolution

When two regions cover the same pixel, `overlap` decides who wins. The ROIs are
rasterised in draw order (ascending `z`, then insertion):

```{r overlap}
lyr <- at_layer("regions")
lyr <- at_layer_add(lyr, at_roi_rect(1, 1, 5, 5, label = "a"))
lyr <- at_layer_add(lyr, at_roi_rect(3, 3, 7, 7, label = "b"))
matrix(as.integer(at_mask(lyr, "labelled", dims = c(8, 8), overlap = "last")),  8, 8)
matrix(as.integer(at_mask(lyr, "labelled", dims = c(8, 8), overlap = "first")), 8, 8)
```

`"last"` (the default) lets the later-drawn region overwrite; `"first"` keeps
the earlier one; `"max"` and `"min"` resolve by pixel value; and `"error"`
aborts the moment any two regions collide, which is the safest choice when
overlaps should never happen.

`"bitor"` keeps every membership instead of choosing a winner. It is meant for
multiclass masks whose class codes are distinct powers of two: an overlapping
pixel holds the bitwise OR of the codes, so a pixel covered by `a` (1) and `b`
(2) holds 3 and both classes stay recoverable with `bitwAnd()`.

```{r bitor}
bits <- at_mask(lyr, "multiclass", dims = c(8, 8), values = c(a = 1L, b = 2L),
                overlap = "bitor")
matrix(as.integer(bits), 8, 8)
at_mask_legend(bits)[, c("value", "label", "n_px")]
```

## Masks from a project

On a real project the mask spans the image grid. The bundled example carries one
layer of three labelled regions:

```{r project}
proj <- at_example_project()
mc <- at_mask(proj, type = "multiclass")
mc
at_mask_legend(mc)
table(as.integer(mc))
```

`at_mask_stats()` summarises each value — pixel counts, area, fraction of the
frame, bounding box and centroid — ready for a report table:

```{r stats}
at_mask_stats(mc)
```

## Writing masks and the legend sidecar

`at_write_mask()` writes an integer TIFF (16-bit by default), and — because a
bare integer raster is meaningless without a key — a companion
`<path>.legend.json` describing it:

```{r write}
dir  <- tempfile("masks-"); dir.create(dir)
path <- file.path(dir, "regions.tif")
at_write_mask(mc, path, overwrite = TRUE)
list.files(dir)
cat(readLines(paste0(path, ".legend.json")), sep = "\n")
```

The sidecar is self-describing. Its fields, printed above, include the
`annotatR_version`, the `created` timestamp, the `mask_type`, the pyramid
`level`, the raster `dims`, the `source_project`, and the full `legend` array
(one object per value, mirroring the legend tibble).
The sidecar also contains `mask_metadata` schema 1. NPY sidecars separately
record `storage$axes` (`yx` or `xy`) and `storage$shape`; these describe the array
on disk, while the metadata grid describes logical image samples. For a
transposed NPY export, read with `at_read_npy(..., transpose = TRUE)`. A mismatched
explicit orientation fails even when a square shape would conceal the error.
`at_read_mask()` recovers the declared NPY orientation automatically.
Any consumer can map pixel values back to labels without touching R.

TIFF export accepts `bits = 8L` or `bits = 16L` (the default) and preserves
unsigned integer class codes in `[0, 255]` or `[0, 65535]`. PNG export remains
8-bit only: values above 255 and all negative values reject before writing.
`bits` controls TIFF only. Both formats reject fractional/nonfinite samples
and out-of-range values before creating or overwriting the destination.
TIFF writing needs `tiff` or a `magick` build with exact grayscale support;
PNG needs the latter. An unavailable lossless writer produces a capability
error. Single-choice arguments require a scalar: omitted defaults choose the
first documented value, while explicitly supplied vectors are invalid.

## Downstream consumption

A Python pipeline reads the TIFF and its legend directly — no R runtime, no
bespoke format:

```python
import json
import tifffile

mask = tifffile.imread("regions.tif")            # integer array, image grid
with open("regions.tif.legend.json") as f:
    legend = json.load(f)

value_to_label = {row["value"]: row["label"] for row in legend["legend"]}
tumour = mask == next(v for v, l in value_to_label.items() if l == "tumour")
```

## Reading masks back

Masks are not a dead end. `at_read_mask()` polygonises an existing mask —
hyperannotatR's own output, or a Cellpose/StarDist/QuPath raster — back into an
editable `annot_layer`, recovering labels from the sidecar when it is present:

```{r read}
back <- at_read_mask(path)
vapply(back$rois, function(r) r$label, character(1))
```

Recovery precedence is explicit arguments, embedded RDS metadata, then sidecar.
`legend` and `level` override the corresponding fields of an optional
`metadata` list. For example, a known legacy bitfield can be imported with
`metadata = list(encoding = "bitfield", overlap = "bitor")` and a supplied
legend of its base bits. Overrides do not resample the array. Legacy masks
without sufficient encoding metadata default to exclusive instance/categorical
values and background zero, with `status = "legacy-default"`; composite values
missing from a legacy legend fail instead of being guessed as bits. Signed
representable integer categories are valid. Corrupt dimensions, noninteger
samples, malformed legends, and unknown schema versions fail explicitly.
Sampled previews and translated grids cannot be polygonised into editable ROIs;
import the original-resolution mask with unit stride and zero origin instead.
Their sampled arrays remain available through `at_read_npy()`, preview, and
statistics APIs.
TIFF masks must be a single two-dimensional integer plane; fractional samples
and multiple planes are rejected before conversion. Raw TIFF import requires
`tiff`; it does not fall back to display grayscale conversion. PNG import
preserves unsigned 8/16-bit grayscale class codes, including 65535, using a
`magick` build that passes an exact grayscale capability check. Palette, RGB,
alpha-bearing, grayscale `tRNS` transparency and other-depth PNGs reject before
polygonisation. A transparency key is rejected even if none of the stored
samples use that key.

`connectivity = 8L` (default) joins pixels that share a corner or edge into
one ROI. `connectivity = 4L` joins only edge neighbours. Point-touching parts
of an eight-connected region are retained together as valid multipart
geometry with the same pixel membership. Connectivity must be a single
finite whole number; missing, fractional, other-valued or explicit vector
arguments are invalid.

Finally, `at_plot_mask()` renders a mask with its legend for a quick visual
check:

```{r plot}
at_plot_mask(mc)
```
